tool.name: IdentifyTerminiPolygons
tool.summary: Finds the corridor termini polygons within each Wildland Block: the concentrations of a quality surface -- a species habitat-suitability surface, a Land Facet Density raster, or a Diversity surface -- that the least-cost corridors will run between. Cells above a threshold are aggregated into regions -- touching along an edge or at a corner counts as connected -- and each Wildland Block keeps the regions at least a given percentage (default 50%) of the size of its largest region. A third option skips thresholding entirely and uses each Wildland Block polygon itself as its own terminus. Fed a multi-band Land Facet Density raster it processes every category in one run and writes one polygon feature class with a Category field. Any number of Wildland Block features is allowed. A modernized, generalized port of the Land Facet Corridor Designer's Identify Termini Polygons tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
Why termini. A land facet corridor does not run from the edge of one Wildland Block to the edge of the other -- it runs between the concentrations of the facet inside the blocks (Land Facet Corridor Designer manual, pp. 44-46). If a block held no meaningful concentration of the facet, there would be nothing for the corridor to connect. This tool finds those concentrations, called termini: for each Wildland Block it takes the cells of the analysis surface above a threshold, aggregates them into regions, and keeps the regions large enough to be worth connecting.
The analysis surface. This is not a Land-Facet-only tool. Its traditional and still most common use, the one CorridorDesigner was originally built for, is a species habitat suitability surface: high values mean good habitat, and the median threshold rule below finds the best half of each block's own ground. The suite's Land Facet chain uses the same mechanism differently: (1) a Land Facet Density raster from this suite's Land Facet Density tool -- the tool reads the band-to-facet mapping from the raster's own records, converts the stored integer values back to 0-1 proportions, analyzes every facet (band) in one run, and labels each terminus with its facet, so one run of this tool replaces the original's one-run-per-facet workflow (use the "Categories / bands to analyze" parameter to restrict the run); or (2) a Diversity surface (Diversity Indices tool, Shannon's index or the effective number of species), for the facet-interspersion corridor. Any other single-band raster where high values mean "good" works identically to a habitat-suitability surface.
The threshold. Three rules. Fixed value keeps cells whose value is strictly greater than the number you give; the manual recommends 0 for density surfaces, meaning any cell with any density at all is eligible. Median within each Wildland Block implements the manual's diversity rule exactly -- and works the same way for a habitat-suitability surface, keeping each block's own best half: page 13 defines the diversity termini as "the half of all cells inside each Wildland Block with the highest H'" -- that is, each block's threshold is the median of its own cells, computed here per block automatically. (The original tool asked for a single hand-computed number, and a median taken from the whole raster -- including everything outside the blocks -- is not the published rule.) The threshold each region had to beat is written to its Threshold field. Treat entire block polygons as Termini polygons skips thresholding altogether: each Wildland Block polygon is written directly as its own single terminus. This is the simplest possible baseline -- connect the protected areas directly, with no attempt to target a quality concentration inside them -- and it is also how Least-Cost Corridor can be used with no quality surface at all; the Relative Size Threshold parameter has no effect in this mode. The rule is pre-selected for you when the input's own records identify it: choosing a Land Facet Density raster sets the fixed rule with threshold 0, and choosing a Diversity Indices surface sets the per-block median rule -- either can then be overridden by hand (the whole-block rule is always a manual choice).
Aggregation and the size rule. Cells above the threshold that touch along an edge or at a corner belong to the same region (the manual's stated rule, step 2, page 44). Within each Wildland Block the tool finds the largest region, and keeps every region whose area is at least the Relative size threshold percentage of it -- at the default 50%, a region half the size of the block's biggest concentration survives, a small island does not. Each facet is judged independently, and each block is judged independently: the comparison group is always "regions of this facet in this block". Areas are measured geodesically (square meters) after clipping each region to its block boundary, so the comparison is honest on geographic (latitude-longitude) rasters where the original compared square degrees.
The Wildland Blocks. Any polygon layer; every feature is one block, analyzed separately (a selection on the layer is honored). The original required exactly two polygons and made you Append/Merge/Dissolve your data into that shape; this version simply takes what you have -- two blocks for a classic corridor, or more for a multi-linkage design. If your blocks are multi-part after a Dissolve, run Multipart To Singlepart first so each block is its own feature. Overlapping block features draw a warning (a cell can only be analyzed as part of one block). Blocks in a different coordinate system are projected to the raster's automatically.
The output. One polygon feature class holding every category's termini together, in the raster's coordinate system. Fields: Category (the category's label, from the source raster's records -- group or filter by this field to recover the per-category termini; named Category rather than Facet because this tool is just as much for species habitat-suitability surfaces as for land facets), CategoryID, Block (which Wildland Block feature, 1-based in the block layer's feature order), Terminus (sequential number), Area_SqM (geodesic square meters, after clipping to the block), Cells (raster cells above the threshold in the region), PctOfMax (the region's size as a percentage of its block's largest region -- 100 marks each block's biggest terminus), MeanValue and MaxValue (the analysis surface over the region's cells; density values are reported as 0-1 proportions), and Threshold. The output draws with a unique-values symbology on the Category field, and carries a linkage record of its place in the analysis chain -- the Least-Cost Corridor tool reads the Category and Block fields to build every category's corridor in one run, and the Corridor Analysis Data Report can describe the output's full lineage.
When a category cannot anchor a corridor. A corridor needs a terminus at both ends. A category can end up with termini in only some of the Wildland Blocks -- no cells exceeded the threshold in a block, or every region there was clipped away -- and such a category has nothing to connect to in the missing block. The tool warns about every such category in its run messages (naming the blocks with and without termini), records the per-category per-block terminus counts in the output's linkage record, and the Corridor Analysis Data Report displays those counts and repeats the warning, so the gap is visible long after the run messages are gone.
Fixes to the original, for the record. The ArcMap original had a wrong-variable bug (LandFacetFunctions.bas line 363) that skipped Wildland Block 2's clipping and size filtering whenever Block 1 had no eligible cells, writing Block 2's polygons raw; this version processes every block independently and correctly. It also needed Spatial Analyst; this version needs none.
References. Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010. Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors. Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2009.01422.x). Brost, B. M., and P. Beier. 2012. Use of land facets to design linkages for climate change. Ecological Applications 22:87-103 (https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0213.1). Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013. Land Facet Corridor Designer. http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm.

param.name: in_raster
param.displayname: Analysis surface (density, diversity or HSI raster)

dialogReference.para: The surface whose concentrations become the termini. A multi-band Land Facet Density raster is analyzed facet by facet in one run (the band-to-facet mapping and the stored-integer scaling come from the raster's own records, so thresholds are in true 0-1 proportions); a Diversity surface or any other single-band raster where high values are good works the same way. A single band of a density raster can also be given directly (for example dens.tif\Band_3).

param.name: blocks
param.displayname: Wildland Block polygons (each feature = one block)

dialogReference.para: The Wildland Blocks the corridor will connect. Every feature is one block, analyzed separately; any number of features is allowed (the original tool's exactly-two-polygons requirement is lifted), and a selection on the layer is honored. Blocks in a different coordinate system are projected to the raster's automatically. Overlapping features draw a warning.

The termini polygons, all categories together, in the raster's coordinate system. Fields: Category, CategoryID, Block, Terminus, Area_SqM, Cells, PctOfMax, MeanValue, MaxValue, Threshold -- each documented in the output's field metadata. A name is suggested from the input. The layer draws with unique-values symbology on the Category field.
How the eligibility threshold is chosen.

bulletList.bullet_item: Fixed value keeps cells strictly greater than the Threshold value parameter -- use 0 for density surfaces, so any cell with any density at all is eligible.

Median within each Wildland Block computes each block's own median from its own cells and keeps the upper half -- the manual's rule for diversity surfaces, and equally useful for a species habitat-suitability surface (each block's own best half), computed exactly rather than hand-approximated.
Treat entire block polygons as Termini polygons skips thresholding: each Wildland Block polygon becomes its own single terminus, with no quality surface needed to target a concentration within it.

dialogReference.para: The rule is pre-selected automatically when the input carries one of this suite's density or diversity records (fixed 0 for density, per-block median for diversity); your own choice afterward is respected, and the whole-block rule is always a manual choice.

The fixed threshold: cells strictly greater than this value are eligible. The default 0 is the manual's recommendation for density surfaces. For a density raster the value is in true proportions (0 to 1), not stored integers. Ignored in median mode and in whole-block mode.

param.name: relative_size_pct
param.displayname: Relative size threshold (% of the largest polygon in each block)

dialogReference.para: How large a region must be, as a percentage of the largest region of the same facet in the same Wildland Block, to be kept as a terminus (0-100; default 50, the original's default). At 0 every region is kept; at 100 only each block's largest region (and exact ties) survives. Has no effect in whole-block mode, where every block is kept by definition.
For a multi-band input, restricts the run to these categories (listed from the density raster's own records) or band numbers. Leave empty to analyze every band.

scriptExample.title: Identify Termini Polygons example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Termini of every facet of a density raster at the manual's defaults; a species habitat-suitability surface with the per-block median rule; and the whole-block shortcut with no quality surface at all. threshold_mode values are exactly: "Fixed value (density surfaces: 0)", "Median within each Wildland Block (diversity and habitat suitability surfaces)", "Treat entire block polygons as Termini polygons".
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Every facet of a Land Facet Density raster: any density at all is eligible, # keep regions at least half the size of each block's largest. arcpy.jenness.IdentifyTerminiPolygons( r"C:\data\out.gdb\LandFacetDensity", r"C:\data\out.gdb\WildlandBlocks", r"C:\data\out.gdb\Facet_Termini", "Fixed value (density surfaces: 0)", 0, 50)
# A species habitat-suitability surface: each block's own best half, # computed automatically. arcpy.jenness.IdentifyTerminiPolygons( r"C:\data\out.gdb\Species_HSM", r"C:\data\out.gdb\WildlandBlocks", r"C:\data\out.gdb\Species_Termini", "Median within each Wildland Block (diversity and habitat suitability surfaces)", None, 50)
# No quality surface at all: the Wildland Blocks themselves become the # Least-Cost Corridor input. arcpy.jenness.IdentifyTerminiPolygons( r"C:\data\out.gdb\Species_HSM", r"C:\data\out.gdb\WildlandBlocks", r"C:\data\out.gdb\Block_Termini", "Treat entire block polygons as Termini polygons", None, None)
